attribution.note: Marcus's own prose. It follows Rosenzweig's annotations, but the bait-and-switch passage is his.

semantics.note: Faithful. Drops 'just' and the 'promises to serve all humanity' framing, which is rhetorical. The two empirical parts are kept.

contract.note: The plain reading is ordinary. Choosing calendar 2023 and requiring matched denominators is reasonable, but the result depends on undefined terms: mostly, small, chatbots, and charitable work.

evidence.note: DevDay 2023 lists TTS, image and vision products. It qualifies 'just chatbots' but gives no revenue shares.
Grant program announced in 2023 at $100k per recipient. It shows charitable activity exists, but there is no operating denominator.

The 2023 Form 990 for the nonprofit parent shows about $2.7M in program expenses and more than $15M in grants and credits via related entities. Its scope is the parent entity, not consolidated OpenAI.

reviews.rationale: The packet has no 2023 product revenue breakdown and no consolidated spending breakdown. The parent-only 990 figures suggest charitable work was small, but the contract forbids dividing them by group totals. Product diversity alone does not show whether chatbots dominated sales. Neither condition can be established.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his post.

semantics.note: Revision 2 keeps the year scope, 'many', the ongoing erosion, and 'sometimes ... significantly lower prices'.

contract.note: Counting large context, vision input and capability gains as a major update is an ordinary informed reading. It is not stretched. Marcus may have meant a GPT-5-class leap, but he did not say so.

evidence.note: GPT-4 Turbo (Nov 2023, within the year): more capable, 128K context, vision in the API, cheaper. This is a substantial update.
Claude 3 (Mar 2024) offers overlapping chat and API products with strong benchmark results. These are vendor claims, and the excerpt does not show prices.
Gemini (Dec 2023): vendor benchmarks show competitive capability. This is a company disclosure.
Mistral Large (Feb 2024) is an API and chat competitor that ranks itself just behind GPT-4. Vendor claim.

Independent Arena-Hard results: Claude 3 Opus exceeds the original GPT-4, but the Turbo variants lead by a wide margin. This supports convergence with the original model and also shows Turbo's gains. There is a judge-bias caveat.

reviews.rationale: The no-major-update clause is contradicted by GPT-4 Turbo's November 2023 release, which brought capability, context and modality gains. The competitor clauses largely hold: Claude 3, Gemini and Mistral offered overlapping products, and independent data shows Claude 3 Opus surpassing the original GPT-4. Lower-priced rival tiers are asserted but only weakly shown in the excerpts.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his post.

semantics.note: The 'does not appear' hedge on the GPT-5 clause is preserved. The agent clause is firm. The as-of date matches 'thus far' at publication.

contract.note: Reading 'reliable agent' as dependable multi-step execution is ordinary. The GPT-5 clause is hedged ('does not seem'), and the contract rightly treats absence of a release as not proving absence of a model.

evidence.note: GPTs with actions (Nov 2023). OpenAI says real-world tasks will come 'eventually'. This shows agent-like features, not reliability.
Assistants API described as a 'first step' toward agent-like experiences. Reliability is not quantified.
Ars relays anonymous reports of GPT-5 previews and calls it a rumor. No verified capability evidence.

reviews.rationale: The packet shows agent-like tools but no reliability record either way. OpenAI's own wording points to the agent goal being unmet, but that is not a complete demonstration record. The GPT-5 clause is hedged, and the only evidence on it is unverified rumor. Neither the support nor the contradiction condition is met.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words. The rhetorical question presupposes non-payment. Mapping Altman to OpenAI is reasonable.

semantics.note: Pulls the factual presuppositions out of the rhetorical question. 'Fleecing' is evaluative and rightly left unscored. '(to most)' is kept.

contract.note: Treating 'a lot' as substantial documented instances is fair and ordinary. Requiring a creator-level denominator for 'most' is strict but faithful to the words.

evidence.note: April 2024 SoA survey: 36% of translators report losing work to generative AI. This backs the lost-gigs clause, but it is self-reported and not tied to OpenAI.
2023 OpenAI disclosure: most data comes from public sources. No count of creators or payments, and it predates the target period.
FT licensing deal (Apr 2024): a publisher was paid. It does not show whether individual creators were paid or what share.

reviews.rationale: The lost-gigs clause is supported by the contemporaneous SoA survey. The packet cannot settle the compensation clause: there is no creator-level denominator or payment record, and the FT deal shows only a publisher-level payment. Since one clause is unsettled, the support condition is not met overall and nothing contradicts the claim.
